statement: Let $I$ be an open interval and $f_n\colon I\to\mathbb{R}$ differentiable. If $f_n\to g$ [pointwise](c:pointwise-convergence) on $I$ and $f_n'\to h$ [uniformly](c:uniform-convergence) on $I$, then $g$ is differentiable on $I$ with [derivative](c:derivative) $g'=h$.

hypotheses.text: Each $f_n$ is differentiable on $I$ with [derivative](c:derivative) $f_n'$.
The sequence $f_n$ converges [pointwise](c:pointwise-convergence) to $g$ on $I$.
The derivatives $f_n'$ converge [uniformly](c:uniform-convergence) on $I$ to a function $h$.

conclusion: The function $g$ is differentiable at every $x\in I$ and $g'(x)=h(x)$.

formal.difference: The declaration takes a normed space over the reals or complex numbers as domain, values in a normed space, and any filter in place of $n\to\infty$. The open-set form is hasFDerivAt_of_tendstoUniformlyOn.

proofs.name: Uniform difference quotients
proofs.slogan: Show that the difference quotients of $f_n$ converge uniformly, then split the error into three small terms.
proofs.scope: The whole statement at one fixed point $x\in I$; the open interval $I$ is convex, so the segment from $x$ to $y$ stays in $I$.

roles.why: Differentiability of $f_n-f_m$ allows the mean value theorem, and differentiability of $f_n$ at $x$ controls the last term.
Pointwise limits turn the Cauchy bound on quotients into a bound for the quotient of $g$.
Uniform convergence makes the derivatives uniformly Cauchy and close to $h$ at $x$.

steps.slogan: Bound the difference of two difference quotients by the derivative gap.
steps.detail: Fix $x\in I$ and put $q_n(y)=\frac{f_n(y)-f_n(x)}{y-x}$ for $y\ne x$. The mean value theorem for $f_n-f_m$ gives $|q_n(y)-q_m(y)|\le\sup_I|f_n'-f_m'|$.

steps.slogan: Make the difference quotients uniformly Cauchy in $y$.
steps.detail: The derivatives converge [uniformly](c:uniform-convergence), so for $\varepsilon>0$ there is $N$ with $\sup_I|f_n'-f_m'|\le\varepsilon$ for $n,m\ge N$. Step 1 gives $|q_n(y)-q_m(y)|\le\varepsilon$ for all $y\ne x$ and $n,m\ge N$.

steps.slogan: Let $m$ tend to infinity to bound $q_n-q$ uniformly.
steps.detail: Pointwise convergence gives $q_m(y)\to q(y)=\frac{g(y)-g(x)}{y-x}$. Letting $m\to\infty$ in step 2 gives $|q_n(y)-q(y)|\le\varepsilon$ for all $y\ne x$ and $n\ge N$.

steps.slogan: Split $q(y)-h(x)$ into three terms and choose $n$.
steps.detail: Write $|q(y)-h(x)|\le|q(y)-q_n(y)|+|q_n(y)-f_n'(x)|+|f_n'(x)-h(x)|$. The first term is at most $\varepsilon$ by step 3. Fix $n\ge N$ so large that the third term is below $\varepsilon$.

steps.slogan: Shrink $y$ toward $x$ so that the middle term is small.
steps.detail: Since $f_n$ is [differentiable](c:derivative) at $x$, there is $\delta>0$ with $|q_n(y)-f_n'(x)|<\varepsilon$ for $0<|y-x|<\delta$. Then $|q(y)-h(x)|<3\varepsilon$ for these $y$, so $g'(x)=h(x)$.

concepts.c:uniform-convergence: Uniform convergence of $f_n'$ makes the quotients uniformly Cauchy.
concepts.c:pointwise-convergence: Pointwise convergence defines $g$ and the limit quotient $q$.
concepts.c:derivative: The derivative is the limit of the difference quotient that the proof controls.

source.note: mathlib shows that the difference quotients converge uniformly (uniformCauchySeqOnFilter_of_fderiv, difference_quotients_converge_uniformly) and finishes with an epsilon/3 split in hasFDerivAt_of_tendstoUniformlyOnFilter.

statement: Let $f_n$ be differentiable on an open interval $I$ with a [summable bound](c:summable-bound) $|f_n'|\le u_n$ on $I$. If the [series](c:series) $\sum f_n(x_0)$ converges at one point $x_0\in I$, then $\sum f_n$ converges on $I$ and its sum is differentiable with derivative $\sum f_n'$.

hypotheses.text: Each $f_n\colon I\to\mathbb{R}$ is [differentiable](c:differentiable-function) on the open interval $I$.
The derivatives have a [summable bound](c:summable-bound): $|f_n'(x)|\le u_n$ for all $n$ and $x\in I$, and $\sum u_n$ converges.
The [series](c:series) $\sum f_n(x_0)$ converges for one point $x_0\in I$.

conclusion: The series $\sum f_n(x)$ converges for every $x\in I$, and its sum $F$ is differentiable with $F'=\sum f_n'$.

formal.difference: The declaration drops the hypothesis at $x_0$, because mathlib gives a non-summable sum the value $0$, and it states differentiability without the formula for the derivative. It works on a normed space with values in a Banach space; the formula is hasFDerivAt_tsum.

proofs.name: Limit of partial sums
proofs.slogan: Prove uniform convergence of the derivative series and pointwise convergence of the series, then differentiate the limit of the partial sums.
proofs.scope: The whole statement for real functions on an open interval; the declaration's case of no convergence anywhere is excluded by the hypothesis at $x_0$.

roles.why: Differentiable terms make each partial sum differentiable with the sum of the derivatives.
The bound $u_n$ gives the uniform tail estimate and the comparison for the series.
Convergence at $x_0$ is the base point that the mean value estimate transfers to every $x$.

steps.slogan: Show that the partial sums of $\sum f_n'$ converge uniformly on $I$.
steps.detail: Let $G(x)=\sum f_n'(x)$, which converges absolutely by comparison with $\sum u_n$. The tail satisfies $|G(x)-\sum_{n<N}f_n'(x)|\le\sum_{n\ge N}u_n$, which tends to $0$ independently of $x$.

steps.slogan: Show that the series $\sum f_n$ converges at every point of $I$.
steps.detail: The mean value theorem gives $|f_n(x)-f_n(x_0)|\le u_n|x-x_0|$. Comparison with $\sum u_n|x-x_0|$ shows that $\sum(f_n(x)-f_n(x_0))$ converges, and so does $\sum f_n(x)$.

steps.slogan: Differentiate the partial sums and pass to the limit.
steps.detail: Each partial sum $S_N=\sum_{n<N}f_n$ is differentiable with $S_N'=\sum_{n<N}f_n'$. By steps 1 and 2, $S_N\to F$ pointwise and $S_N'\to G$ uniformly, so the limit theorem for derivatives gives $F'=G$ on $I$.

concepts.c:summable-bound: The summable bound controls both the derivative tails and the series terms.
concepts.c:series: The theorem concerns the convergence and the sum of the series.
concepts.c:differentiable-function: Differentiable terms give differentiable partial sums.

source.note: mathlib proves hasFDerivAt_tsum: the partial sums converge uniformly in derivative (tendstoUniformlyOn_tsum) and hasFDerivAt_of_tendstoUniformlyOn passes to the limit; differentiable_tsum adds the no-convergence case.

statement: Let $X$ be a [compact space](c:compact-space) and $f_n\colon X\to\mathbb{R}$ [continuous](c:continuous-function) with $f_n\le f_{n+1}$. If $f_n$ converges pointwise to a continuous function $f$, then $f_n\to f$ [uniformly](c:uniform-convergence) on $X$.

hypotheses.text: The space $X$ is [compact](c:compact-space).
Each $f_n\colon X\to\mathbb{R}$ is [continuous](c:continuous-function).
The sequence is [monotone](c:monotone-sequence): $f_n(x)\le f_{n+1}(x)$ for all $n$ and $x$.
The sequence converges [pointwise](c:pointwise-convergence): $f_n(x)\to f(x)$ for every $x\in X$.
The limit function $f$ is [continuous](c:continuous-function).

formal.difference: The declaration gives locally uniform convergence on any topological space, for an index preorder and values in a normed lattice. Uniform convergence on a compact space is the companion declaration Monotone.tendstoUniformly_of_forall_tendsto.

proofs.name: Finite subcover of small gaps
proofs.slogan: Find a neighborhood of each point where the gap to the limit is small for all later indices, then cover the compact space by finitely many.
proofs.scope: The whole statement for an increasing sequence; a decreasing sequence follows by replacing $f_n$ and $f$ with $-f_n$ and $-f$.

roles.why: Compactness turns the local neighborhoods into a finite family, hence one index $N$.
The continuous $f_{n_x}$ makes the set where the gap is small open.
Monotonicity keeps the gap small for all later indices and fixes its sign.
Pointwise convergence gives, at each point, an index with a small gap.
Continuity of $f$ makes the gap $f-f_{n_x}$ continuous.

steps.slogan: Show that every $f_n$ lies below the limit $f$.
steps.detail: For fixed $x$ the real sequence $f_m(x)$ is increasing with limit $f(x)$, so $f_n(x)\le f(x)$ for every $n$. Hence the gaps $f-f_n$ are nonnegative and decrease as $n$ grows.

steps.slogan: Choose, for each point, an index with a small gap.
steps.detail: Fix $\varepsilon>0$. For each $x\in X$ [pointwise](c:pointwise-convergence) convergence gives an index $n_x$ with $f(x)-f_{n_x}(x)<\varepsilon$.

steps.slogan: Spread the small gap over an open neighborhood of each point.
steps.detail: The function $f-f_{n_x}$ is [continuous](c:continuous-function), so $U_x=\{y: f(y)-f_{n_x}(y)<\varepsilon\}$ is open and contains $x$. For $m\ge n_x$ and $y\in U_x$, monotonicity gives $0\le f(y)-f_m(y)\le f(y)-f_{n_x}(y)<\varepsilon$.

steps.slogan: Select a finite subcover of the open cover $\{U_x\}$.
steps.detail: The sets $U_x$ cover the [compact space](c:compact-space) $X$, so finitely many of them, $U_{x_1},\dots,U_{x_k}$, cover $X$. Put $N=\max_i n_{x_i}$.

steps.slogan: Take the largest index to bound the gap on all of $X$.
steps.detail: Let $m\ge N$ and $y\in X$. Choose $i$ with $y\in U_{x_i}$; then $m\ge n_{x_i}$, so $0\le f(y)-f_m(y)<\varepsilon$. Hence $\sup_X|f-f_m|\le\varepsilon$ for all $m\ge N$.

concepts.c:compact-space: Compactness gives a finite subcover, so finitely many indices suffice.
concepts.c:continuous-function: Continuity makes the set of small gap values open.
concepts.c:monotone-sequence: Monotonicity keeps the gap small for every later index.
concepts.c:pointwise-convergence: Pointwise convergence gives an index with a small gap at each point.
concepts.c:uniform-convergence: Uniform convergence is the conclusion, one index for all points.

source.note: mathlib shows F n x ≤ f x with ge_of_tendsto, then uses isOpen_lt for the open set where the gap is below epsilon; compactness gives Monotone.tendstoUniformly_of_forall_tendsto.

statement: Let $a_n$ be terms in a [complete](c:complete-metric-space) normed space and $b_n$ real numbers with $\|a_n\|\le b_n$ for all $n$. If the [series](c:series) $\sum b_n$ converges, then $\sum a_n$ converges.

hypotheses.text: The terms satisfy $\|a_n\|\le b_n$ for every $n$.
The [series](c:series) $\sum b_n$ of real numbers converges.
The normed space that holds the terms $a_n$ is [complete](c:complete-metric-space), for example $\mathbb{R}$ or $\mathbb{C}$.

formal.difference: The declaration states only that the partial sums of $\sum a_n$ form a Cauchy sequence, in any seminormed group. Convergence needs completeness, which is the hypothesis here.

proofs.name: Cauchy blocks
proofs.slogan: Bound each block of terms $a_k$ by the same block of $b_k$, so the partial sums are Cauchy, and use completeness.
proofs.scope: The whole statement; if the bound holds only from some index on, the finitely many early terms do not change convergence.

roles.why: The bound $\|a_k\|\le b_k$ moves the estimate from $a$-blocks to $b$-blocks.
Convergence of $\sum b_n$ makes its tails small.
Completeness turns a Cauchy sequence of partial sums into a limit.

steps.slogan: Show that the tails of $\sum b_n$ are small.
steps.detail: A convergent real series satisfies the Cauchy criterion. So for $\varepsilon>0$ there is $N$ with $\sum_{k=m}^{n-1}b_k<\varepsilon$ for $n>m\ge N$.

steps.slogan: Bound each block of $a$-terms by the same block of $b$-terms.
steps.detail: For $n>m$ the triangle inequality gives $\|\sum_{k=m}^{n-1}a_k\|\le\sum_{k=m}^{n-1}\|a_k\|$. The hypothesis $\|a_k\|\le b_k$ bounds this by $\sum_{k=m}^{n-1}b_k$.

steps.slogan: Conclude that the partial sums of $\sum a_n$ are Cauchy.
steps.detail: Put $A_n=\sum_{k<n}a_k$. For $n>m\ge N$, steps 1 and 2 give $\|A_n-A_m\|\le\sum_{k=m}^{n-1}b_k<\varepsilon$, so $(A_n)$ is a [Cauchy sequence](c:cauchy-sequence).

steps.slogan: Take the limit of the Cauchy sequence in the complete space.
steps.detail: The space is [complete](c:complete-metric-space), so $(A_n)$ converges to some $A$. This says that the series $\sum a_n$ converges to $A$.

concepts.c:series: The theorem compares two series through their partial sums.
concepts.c:complete-metric-space: Completeness gives the limit of the Cauchy partial sums.
concepts.c:cauchy-sequence: The partial sums of $\sum a_n$ are shown to be Cauchy.

source.note: mathlib uses Metric.cauchySeq_iff', sum_Ico_eq_sub, norm_sum_le and sum_le_sum to bound each block of f by the same block of g.

statement: Let $A\colon[0,T]\to M_n(\mathbb{C})$ be continuous and let $U$ solve the [ordinary differential equation](c:ordinary-differential-equation) $U'=AU$, $U(0)=1$. Then $U(t)=\sum_{k\ge0}\int_{t\ge t_1\ge\dots\ge t_k\ge0}A(t_1)\cdots A(t_k)\,dt_1\cdots dt_k$, the [time-ordered exponential](c:time-ordered-exponential) of $A$, and the series converges uniformly.

hypotheses.text: The matrix function $A\colon[0,T]\to M_n(\mathbb{C})$ is continuous.
The function $U\colon[0,T]\to M_n(\mathbb{C})$ is differentiable with $U'(t)=A(t)U(t)$ and $U(0)=1$.

conclusion: For every $t\in[0,T]$, $U(t)$ is the sum of the series of time-ordered integrals, and the series converges uniformly on $[0,T]$.

proofs.name: Picard iteration
proofs.slogan: Iterate the integral equation to get the time-ordered terms, bound them by $(Mt)^k/k!$, sum them and identify the sum with $U$ by uniqueness.
proofs.scope: Matrix-valued $A$ on a compact interval; the same proof works for bounded operators on a Banach space.

roles.why: Continuity makes the integrals exist and gives a finite bound $M$ on $\|A\|$.
The equation $U'=AU$ gives the integral equation that fixes $U$ uniquely.

steps.slogan: Define the iterated integrals by repeated integration.
steps.detail: Put $T_0=1$ and $T_{k+1}(t)=\int_0^tA(s)T_k(s)\,ds$. Unfolding the recursion gives $T_k(t)=\int_{t\ge t_1\ge\dots\ge t_k\ge0}A(t_1)\cdots A(t_k)\,dt$, the $k$-th term of the formula.

steps.slogan: Bound the $k$-th term by $(Mt)^k/k!$ by induction.
steps.detail: Let $M=\max_{[0,T]}\|A\|$, which is finite because $A$ is continuous. The bound holds for $k=0$. If it holds for $k$, then $\|T_{k+1}(t)\|\le\int_0^tM(Ms)^k/k!\,ds=(Mt)^{k+1}/(k+1)!$.

steps.slogan: Sum the series by comparison with the exponential series.
steps.detail: Since $\sum_k(MT)^k/k!=e^{MT}$ converges, the series $V=\sum_kT_k$ converges absolutely and [uniformly](c:uniform-convergence) on $[0,T]$, and $V$ is continuous.

steps.slogan: Show that the sum $V$ solves the differential equation.
steps.detail: Uniform convergence lets the integral pass through the sum: $\int_0^tA\,V\,ds=\sum_k\int_0^tA\,T_k\,ds=\sum_kT_{k+1}(t)=V(t)-1$. So $V=1+\int_0^tAV$, hence $V'=AV$ and $V(0)=1$.

steps.slogan: Identify $U$ with $V$ by uniqueness of solutions.
steps.detail: Integrating $U'=AU$ gives $U=1+\int_0^tAU$. The difference $D=U-V$ then satisfies $\|D(t)\|\le M\int_0^t\|D(s)\|\,ds$, and Grönwall's lemma gives $D=0$. So $U=V$ is the series.

concepts.c:ordinary-differential-equation: The formula solves this linear equation, and uniqueness fixes the solution.
concepts.c:time-ordered-exponential: The series of time-ordered integrals is the time-ordered exponential.
concepts.c:uniform-convergence: Uniform convergence lets the integral pass through the infinite sum.

source.note: Picard iteration of the integral equation, as in the Peano-Baker series of linear ODE theory; the nLab page on the Dyson formula states the result.

statement: Let $T$ be a bounded [self-adjoint operator](c:self-adjoint-operator) on a [Hilbert space](c:hilbert-space) and $x_0\ne0$. If the [Rayleigh quotient](c:rayleigh-quotient) $R(x)=\langle Tx,x\rangle/\|x\|^2$ has a [local extremum](c:local-extremum) at $x_0$ on the sphere $\|x\|=\|x_0\|$, then $x_0$ is an eigenvector of $T$ with eigenvalue $R(x_0)$.

hypotheses.text: The operator $T$ is a bounded [self-adjoint operator](c:self-adjoint-operator) on a [Hilbert space](c:hilbert-space) $H$.
The vector $x_0$ is not zero.
The [Rayleigh quotient](c:rayleigh-quotient) has a [local extremum](c:local-extremum) at $x_0$ on the sphere of radius $\|x_0\|$.

formal.difference: The declaration states the extremum for the form $x\mapsto\operatorname{Re}\langle Tx,x\rangle$ on the sphere, which equals $\|x_0\|^2R$ there, over a real or complex scalar field. It assumes that $H$ is complete, as here.

proofs.name: Lagrange multipliers
proofs.slogan: Treat the sphere as a constraint, obtain Lagrange multipliers for the quadratic form, and solve them into an eigenvalue equation.
proofs.scope: Real or complex scalars; the complex case reduces to the real one in the first step.

roles.why: Self-adjointness makes $\langle Tx,x\rangle$ real and gives the derivative $2\langle Tx_0,\cdot\rangle$.
A nonzero $x_0$ excludes the degenerate multiplier and makes $x_0$ an eigenvector.
The constrained extremum is what the Lagrange rule needs.

steps.slogan: Regard $H$ as a real Hilbert space with the inner product $\operatorname{Re}\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle$.
steps.detail: For self-adjoint $T$ the number $\langle Tx,x\rangle$ is real, so the quadratic form is unchanged. The operator $T$ stays symmetric for the real inner product, and the claim $Tx_0=cx_0$ with real $c$ is the same, so real scalars suffice.

steps.slogan: Compute the derivatives of the quadratic form and of the constraint.
steps.detail: The form $q(x)=\langle Tx,x\rangle$ has derivative $2\langle Tx_0,\cdot\rangle$ at $x_0$, because $T$ is symmetric. The constraint function $\|x\|^2$ has derivative $2\langle x_0,\cdot\rangle$ there.

steps.slogan: Obtain [Lagrange multipliers](c:lagrange-multiplier) $a,b$, not both zero, from the constrained extremum.
steps.detail: At a local extremum of $q$ on the level set of $\|x\|^2$ the two derivatives are linearly dependent. This gives $(a,b)\ne(0,0)$ with $a\langle x_0,\cdot\rangle+b\langle Tx_0,\cdot\rangle=0$, so $ax_0+bTx_0=0$ by the Riesz representation.

steps.slogan: Exclude $b=0$ and solve for $Tx_0$.
steps.detail: If $b=0$, then $a\ne0$ and $ax_0=0$ gives $x_0=0$, against the hypothesis. So $b\ne0$ and $Tx_0=c\,x_0$ with $c=-a/b$.

steps.slogan: Pair the equation with $x_0$ to identify the eigenvalue.
steps.detail: Taking the inner product of $Tx_0=cx_0$ with $x_0$ gives $\langle Tx_0,x_0\rangle=c\|x_0\|^2$, so $c=R(x_0)$. Since $x_0\ne0$, the vector $x_0$ is an eigenvector with this eigenvalue.

concepts.c:self-adjoint-operator: Self-adjointness gives the derivative of the quadratic form.
concepts.c:hilbert-space: The inner product and completeness give the Riesz representation of functionals.
concepts.c:rayleigh-quotient: The quotient is the function whose extremum the hypothesis assumes.
concepts.c:local-extremum: A constrained local extremum is what the multiplier rule needs.
concepts.c:lagrange-multiplier: The multipliers turn the extremum into a linear dependence.
concepts.c:eigenvector: The equation $Tx_0=cx_0$ with $x_0\ne0$ makes $x_0$ an eigenvector.
concepts.c:eigenvalue: The multiplier $c$ is identified with $R(x_0)$ as the eigenvalue.

new_concepts.name: Rayleigh quotient
new_concepts.reminder: The Rayleigh quotient of a self-adjoint operator at a nonzero vector is the normalized quadratic form.
new_concepts.definition: For a bounded self-adjoint operator $T$ on a Hilbert space, the Rayleigh quotient at $x\ne0$ is $R(x)=\langle Tx,x\rangle/\|x\|^2$, a real number.

statement: Let $R,S$ be rings and $F\colon\mathrm{Mod}\text{-}R\to\mathrm{Mod}\text{-}S$ a functor of right modules that preserves [colimits](c:colimit). Then $B=F(R)$ is an $R$-$S$-[bimodule](c:bimodule) and $F\cong-\otimes_RB$, the [tensor product](c:tensor-product) functor. Conversely, every functor $-\otimes_RB$ preserves colimits.

hypotheses.text: The rings $R$ and $S$ have a unit, and the categories are those of right modules.
The functor $F$ preserves all small [colimits](c:colimit).

conclusion: The module $F(R)$ is an $R$-$S$-[bimodule](c:bimodule) $B$, $F(M)\cong M\otimes_RB$ naturally in $M$, and every functor $-\otimes_RB$ preserves colimits.

proofs.name: Watts' argument
proofs.slogan: Make $F(R)$ a bimodule, compare $-\otimes_RF(R)$ with $F$ on free modules, and extend by presentations.
proofs.scope: Right modules over unital rings; the case of left modules is symmetric.

roles.why: The unit makes $R$ a generator, so free modules and presentations exist.
Preserving coproducts and cokernels makes $F$ additive and agree with the tensor functor.

steps.slogan: Make $B=F(R)$ an $R$-$S$-[bimodule](c:bimodule).
steps.detail: The module $F(R)$ is a right $S$-module. For $r\in R$ the map $\lambda_r\colon R\to R$, $x\mapsto rx$, is right $R$-linear, and $r\cdot b=F(\lambda_r)(b)$ defines a left $R$-action that commutes with the $S$-action. The functor $F$ is additive, because it preserves finite coproducts, which are biproducts.

steps.slogan: Define a natural map from $M\otimes_RB$ to $F(M)$.
steps.detail: For $m\in M$ let $\hat m\colon R\to M$, $r\mapsto mr$. The map $(m,b)\mapsto F(\hat m)(b)$ is additive and $R$-balanced, so it gives $\eta_M\colon M\otimes_RB\to F(M)$, natural in $M$ and $S$-linear.

steps.slogan: Show that $\eta$ is an isomorphism on free modules.
steps.detail: For $M=R$ the map $\eta_R\colon R\otimes_RB\to F(R)=B$ is the canonical isomorphism, because $\hat 1=\mathrm{id}_R$. A [free module](c:free-module) $R^{(I)}$ is a coproduct of copies of $R$, and both $F$ and $-\otimes_RB$ preserve coproducts, so $\eta$ is an isomorphism on it.

steps.slogan: Extend the isomorphism to every module by a free presentation.
steps.detail: Choose a presentation $R^{(J)}\to R^{(I)}\to M\to0$. Both functors preserve cokernels, so $\eta_M$ is the map between the cokernels of two isomorphic maps, and it is an isomorphism.

steps.slogan: Prove the converse and the uniqueness of $B$ by adjunction.
steps.detail: The functor $-\otimes_RB$ has the right adjoint $\mathrm{Hom}_S(B,-)$, so it preserves all colimits. Since $R\otimes_RB\cong B$, the bimodule $B$ is determined by the functor as $F(R)$.

concepts.c:colimit: Preserving colimits is the hypothesis that gives additivity and the comparison isomorphism.
concepts.c:bimodule: The bimodule $B$ carries the structure that defines the tensor functor.
concepts.c:tensor-product: The tensor product with $B$ is the functor that equals $F$.
concepts.c:free-module: Free modules are the generators on which the comparison map is checked.

source.note: The argument of C. E. Watts, Intrinsic characterizations of some additive functors, Proc. Amer. Math. Soc. 11 (1960), 5-8, and S. Eilenberg (1960).

statement: A bounded [convex polyhedron](c:convex-polyhedron) in $\mathbb{R}^3$ with $V$ vertices, $E$ edges and $F$ faces satisfies $V-E+F=2$.

hypotheses.text: The solid $P$ is a bounded [convex polyhedron](c:convex-polyhedron) in $\mathbb{R}^3$ with nonempty interior.

conclusion: The numbers of vertices, edges and faces of $P$ satisfy $V-E+F=2$.

proofs.name: Spherical area (Legendre)
proofs.slogan: Project the faces to a sphere, add their areas by Girard's formula, and count angles and sides.
proofs.scope: The whole statement; the value $2$ is the Euler characteristic of the boundary [sphere](c:sphere). Every face is a convex polygon and every edge borders exactly two faces.

roles.why: Convexity gives a radial projection from an interior point that is a bijection onto the sphere.

steps.slogan: Project the boundary radially onto a sphere around an interior point.
steps.detail: Choose an interior point $O$ and project the boundary of $P$ from $O$ onto the unit [sphere](c:sphere). By convexity this is a bijection. An edge and $O$ span a plane through $O$, so edges go to great-circle arcs, and the faces become convex spherical polygons that tile the sphere.

steps.slogan: Express the area of each spherical polygon by its angles.
steps.detail: A spherical $n$-gon with angles $\alpha_1,\dots,\alpha_n$ has area $\sum\alpha_i-(n-2)\pi$. This is Girard's formula for triangles, extended to $n$-gons by cutting them into triangles.

steps.slogan: Add the areas of all faces to get the area of the sphere.
steps.detail: The areas add up to $4\pi$. With $n_f$ the number of sides of face $f$ and $\Sigma$ the sum of all face angles, this reads $4\pi=\Sigma-\pi\sum_fn_f+2\pi F$.

steps.slogan: Count the angles around vertices and the sides of faces.
steps.detail: The face angles at one vertex fill the full angle $2\pi$ around it, so $\Sigma=2\pi V$. Each edge borders exactly two faces, so $\sum_fn_f=2E$.

steps.slogan: Substitute the counts and solve for $V-E+F$.
steps.detail: The sum formula becomes $4\pi=2\pi V-2\pi E+2\pi F$. Dividing by $2\pi$ gives $V-E+F=2$.

concepts.c:convex-polyhedron: Convexity makes the radial projection a bijection and the faces convex.
concepts.c:sphere: The projected faces tile the sphere, whose area is $4\pi$.

source.note: Legendre's proof by spherical area, Elements de geometrie (1794), which rests on Girard's formula for the area of a spherical triangle.

statement: Let $G$ be a finite $n$-player game with [minmax payoffs](c:minmax-payoff) $\underline v_i$. If $v$ is a convex combination of payoff vectors of $G$ with $v_i\ge\underline v_i$ for all $i$, then $v$ is the payoff of a [Nash equilibrium](c:nash-equilibrium) of the infinitely [repeated game](c:repeated-game) with limit-of-means payoffs.

hypotheses.text: The game $G$ is finite with $n$ players, and its [repeated game](c:repeated-game) is played forever with past actions observed.
The vector $v$ is feasible: it is a convex combination of payoff vectors $u(a)$ of pure action profiles $a$.
The vector $v$ is individually rational: $v_i\ge\underline v_i$ for every player $i$, with $\underline v_i$ the [minmax payoff](c:minmax-payoff).

conclusion: The repeated game has a [Nash equilibrium](c:nash-equilibrium) whose payoff vector is $v$.

proofs.name: Trigger strategies
proofs.slogan: Follow a path with average payoff $v$ and punish any deviator forever with the minmax strategy against that player.
proofs.scope: The payoff of a player is the expected limit inferior of the average stage payoff of that player. The discounted and subgame-perfect versions need further arguments, as in Fudenberg and Maskin (1986).

roles.why: Observed past actions let the players detect a deviation and switch to punishment.
Feasibility gives a path of action profiles whose average payoff tends to $v$.
The inequality $v_i\ge\underline v_i$ makes the punishment at least as bad as the path.

steps.slogan: Build a path of action profiles with average payoff tending to $v$.
steps.detail: Write $v=\sum_k\lambda_ku(b^k)$ with pure profiles $b^k$ and weights $\lambda_k\ge0$ that sum to $1$. Play the profiles in blocks of growing length, so that $b^k$ fills a share tending to $\lambda_k$ of the first $T$ periods. The average payoff then tends to $v$.

steps.slogan: Fix a minmax punishment profile against each player.
steps.detail: For each player $i$ let $\alpha^i_{-i}$ be mixed actions of the others with $\max_{a_i}u_i(a_i,\alpha^i_{-i})=\underline v_i$. Against $\alpha^i_{-i}$ player $i$ gets at most $\underline v_i$ per period in expectation, whatever that player does.

steps.slogan: Define the trigger strategies from the path and the punishments.
steps.detail: Each player follows the path $(a^t)$. If player $i$ alone deviates in some period, all others play $\alpha^i_{-i}$ in every later period. Actions are observed, so a deviation from the pure path identifies the deviator.

steps.slogan: Show that no single player gains by deviating.
steps.detail: Say player $i$ first deviates in period $\tau$. The expected stage payoff of player $i$ is at most $\underline v_i$ afterwards, so the expected average of player $i$ up to $T$ is at most $\underline v_i+C\tau/T$. By Fatou's lemma the payoff of player $i$ is at most $\underline v_i\le v_i$.

steps.slogan: Conclude that the strategy profile is a [Nash equilibrium](c:nash-equilibrium) with payoff $v$.
steps.detail: If all players follow the strategies, each gets $v_i$ in the limit. By the previous step no player gains by a single deviation, so the profile is a Nash equilibrium with payoff $v$.

concepts.c:repeated-game: The proof builds strategies for the game repeated forever.
concepts.c:minmax-payoff: The minmax payoff bounds what a deviator gets under punishment.
concepts.c:nash-equilibrium: The strategy profile is shown to be a Nash equilibrium.

source.note: The standard grim-trigger proof, as in M. J. Osborne and A. Rubinstein, A Course in Game Theory (MIT Press, 1994), Chapter 8.

statement: For every $K\ge1$ there are $d(K)$ and $f(K)$ such that every finite set $A\subset\mathbb{Z}$ with [sumset](c:sumset) size $|A+A|\le K|A|$ lies in a [generalized arithmetic progression](c:generalized-arithmetic-progression) of dimension at most $d(K)$ and size at most $f(K)|A|$.

hypotheses.text: The set $A$ is a finite nonempty set of integers.
The [sumset](c:sumset) $A+A$ has at most $K|A|$ elements, for a constant $K\ge1$.

conclusion: The set $A$ lies in a generalized arithmetic progression $P$ with $\dim P\le d(K)$ and $|P|\le f(K)|A|$.

proofs.name: Ruzsa's proof
proofs.slogan: Model the set in a cyclic group, find a large progression in $2A'-2A'$ by Fourier analysis, lift it and cover $A$ by translates.
proofs.scope: An outline of Ruzsa's proof, where the Fourier and geometry-of-numbers steps rest on the cited work. The bounds $d(K)$ and $f(K)$ depend on $K$ only.

roles.why: A finite set embeds by a Freiman isomorphism into a cyclic group of comparable size.
Small doubling bounds all iterated sumsets and the density in the cyclic group.

steps.slogan: Bound all iterated sumsets by the Plünnecke-Ruzsa inequality.
steps.detail: From $|A+A|\le K|A|$ the inequality of Plünnecke and Ruzsa gives $|kA-lA|\le K^{k+l}|A|$ for all $k,l$. In particular $|8A-8A|\le K^{16}|A|$ and $|3A-2A|\le K^5|A|$.

steps.slogan: Model a large part of $A$ inside a cyclic group.
steps.detail: Ruzsa's modeling lemma gives a prime $N>2|8A-8A|$ and a subset $A'\subseteq A$ with $|A'|\ge|A|/8$ that is Freiman-isomorphic of order $8$ to a subset of $\mathbb{Z}/N\mathbb{Z}$. This subset has density at least $c(K)>0$.

steps.slogan: Find a large Bohr set inside $2A'-2A'$ by Fourier analysis.
steps.detail: In $\mathbb{Z}/N\mathbb{Z}$ the set $2A'-2A'$ contains a Bohr set of bounded rank and fixed radius. Bogolyubov's argument gives this from the Fourier transform of the indicator of $A'$.

steps.slogan: Find a proper generalized progression inside the Bohr set.
steps.detail: Geometry of numbers shows that a Bohr set of bounded rank contains a proper [generalized arithmetic progression](c:generalized-arithmetic-progression) $Q$ of bounded dimension and size at least $c'(K)N$.

steps.slogan: Lift the progression to the integers and cover $A$ by translates.
steps.detail: The Freiman isomorphism lifts $Q$ to a progression $P\subseteq2A-2A$ of the same dimension and size. Ruzsa's covering lemma, with $|A+P|\le K^5|A|$, gives a set $X$ of bounded size with $A\subseteq X+P-P$. This set lies in a progression of dimension $\dim P+|X|$ and size at most $2^{\dim P+|X|}|P|$.

concepts.c:sumset: Small sumset size is the doubling hypothesis that every step uses.
concepts.c:generalized-arithmetic-progression: The progression that contains $A$ is the object the theorem produces.

source.ref: I. Z. Ruzsa, Generalized arithmetical progressions and sumsets, Acta Mathematica Hungarica 65 (1994), 379-388
source.note: The outline follows Ruzsa's proof, also presented in T. Tao and V. Vu, Additive Combinatorics (Cambridge University Press, 2006), Chapter 5. The theorem is due to G. A. Freiman (1973).

statement: Let $X$ be an $n$-[connected](c:n-connected-space) pointed [CW complex](c:cw-complex), $n\ge0$. The [suspension](c:suspension) map $E\colon\pi_q(X)\to\pi_{q+1}(\Sigma X)$ on [homotopy groups](c:homotopy-group) is an isomorphism for $q\le2n$ and surjective for $q=2n+1$.

hypotheses.text: The space $X$ is $n$-[connected](c:n-connected-space), that is, $\pi_i(X)=0$ for all $i\le n$, with $n\ge0$.
The space $X$ is a pointed [CW complex](c:cw-complex).

conclusion: The map $E\colon\pi_q(X)\to\pi_{q+1}(\Sigma X)$ is bijective for $q\le2n$ and surjective for $q=2n+1$.

proofs.name: Homotopy excision
proofs.slogan: Write the suspension as two cones glued along $X$ and apply homotopy excision to the pair of cones.
proofs.scope: All $n\ge0$, where $0$-connected means path-connected. The ingredient is the Blakers-Massey excision theorem for homotopy groups.

roles.why: Connectivity of $X$ gives the connectivity of the two pairs of cones and the range of $q$.
The CW structure makes the cones subcomplexes of $\Sigma X$, as excision needs.

steps.slogan: Write $\Sigma X$ as the union of two cones glued along $X$.
steps.detail: The [suspension](c:suspension) is $\Sigma X=C_+X\cup C_-X$ with $C_+X\cap C_-X=X$. Both cones are contractible subcomplexes of the CW complex $\Sigma X$.

steps.slogan: Show that both pairs of a cone and $X$ are $(n+1)$-connected.
steps.detail: The long exact sequence of the pair and the contractibility of the cone give $\pi_i(C_\pm X,X)\cong\pi_{i-1}(X)$. This group vanishes for $i\le n+1$.

steps.slogan: Apply homotopy excision to the triad $(\Sigma X;C_+X,C_-X)$.
steps.detail: Both pairs are $(n+1)$-connected and $X$ is path-connected. The Blakers-Massey theorem then makes $\pi_i(C_+X,X)\to\pi_i(\Sigma X,C_-X)$ bijective for $i<2n+2$ and surjective for $i=2n+2$.

steps.slogan: Identify the resulting composite with the suspension map.
steps.detail: The boundary maps $\pi_{q+1}(C_+X,X)\cong\pi_q(X)$ and $\pi_{q+1}(\Sigma X,C_-X)\cong\pi_{q+1}(\Sigma X)$ are bijections, because the cones are contractible. The composite $\pi_q(X)\to\pi_{q+1}(\Sigma X)$ is the suspension map $E$, up to the sign of the convention.

steps.slogan: Convert the range of $i=q+1$ into the range of $q$.
steps.detail: Put $i=q+1$. Then $i<2n+2$ means $q\le2n$, and $i=2n+2$ means $q=2n+1$. So $E$ is bijective for $q\le2n$ and surjective for $q=2n+1$.

concepts.c:n-connected-space: Connectivity of $X$ sets the connectivity of the pairs and the stable range.
concepts.c:cw-complex: The CW structure makes the cones subcomplexes, which excision needs.
concepts.c:suspension: The suspension is the union of two cones glued along $X$.
concepts.c:homotopy-group: The theorem compares homotopy groups of $X$ and of its suspension.

source.note: A. Hatcher, Algebraic Topology (Cambridge University Press, 2002), Section 4.2, which derives Freudenthal's theorem from homotopy excision.

statement: In a market with finitely many states of positive probability and finitely many trading dates, there is no [arbitrage](c:arbitrage) if and only if some probability $Q$ [equivalent](c:equivalent-measure) to $P$ makes the discounted prices [martingales](c:martingale). Then the market is complete if and only if $Q$ is unique.

hypotheses.text: The probability space $\Omega$ is finite and $P(\omega)>0$ for every state $\omega$.
Trading takes place at finitely many dates, discounted prices are adapted, and strategies are predictable and self-financing.

conclusion: There is no arbitrage if and only if an equivalent martingale measure exists, and then the market is complete if and only if this measure is unique.

proofs.name: Separation of gains
proofs.slogan: Treat the gains of all strategies as a subspace of $\mathbb{R}^\Omega$, separate it from the probability simplex, and read the martingale measure off the separating vector.
proofs.scope: Finite $\Omega$ and a finite horizon, as in Harrison and Pliska. Infinite state spaces and continuous time need the theorems of Dalang, Morton and Willinger and of Delbaen and Schachermayer.

roles.why: Finite dimension, a compact simplex and positive state probabilities make the separation work and give equivalence.
Predictable self-financing strategies give the linear space of gains and the test strategies.

steps.slogan: Collect the gains of all strategies into a linear subspace $K$ of $\mathbb{R}^\Omega$.
steps.detail: A predictable self-financing strategy $H$ has terminal gain $G_H=\sum_tH_t\cdot(S_t-S_{t-1})$. The map $H\mapsto G_H$ is linear, so $K=\{G_H\}$ is a subspace. An [arbitrage](c:arbitrage) is a gain $G\in K$ with $G\ge0$ and $G\ne0$.

steps.slogan: Show that an equivalent martingale measure excludes arbitrage.
steps.detail: Under a [martingale](c:martingale) measure $Q$ each gain satisfies $E_Q[G_H]=0$, being a martingale transform. A gain $G\ge0$ with $E_Q[G]=0$ vanishes in every state, because $Q(\omega)>0$ for all $\omega$.

steps.slogan: Separate $K$ from the simplex of probability vectors.
steps.detail: Without arbitrage, $K$ is disjoint from the compact convex simplex $\Delta=\{x\ge0,\ \sum x_\omega=1\}$. Strict separation gives $y$ with $y\cdot x>0$ on $\Delta$ and $y\cdot k=0$ on $K$, because $K$ is a subspace. Testing vertices gives $y(\omega)>0$ for every $\omega$.

steps.slogan: Normalize $y$ to a measure $Q$ and show that prices are martingales.
steps.detail: Put $Q(\omega)=y(\omega)/\sum y$. Then $Q$ is [equivalent](c:equivalent-measure) to $P$ and $E_Q[G]=0$ on $K$. For a date $t$, an asset $i$ and an event $A\in\mathcal{F}_{t-1}$, the strategy that holds one unit of asset $i$ on $A$ during $(t-1,t]$ gives $E_Q[1_A(S^i_t-S^i_{t-1})]=0$, so $S^i$ is a $Q$-martingale.

steps.slogan: Show that completeness holds exactly when $Q$ is unique.
steps.detail: Attainable claims form the subspace $W=\mathbb{R}+K$, and a martingale measure is a probability with $E_Q[G]=0$ on $K$. If $W=\mathbb{R}^\Omega$, two such measures agree on all indicators. If not, take $z\ne0$ orthogonal to $W$; then $Q+\epsilon z$ is a second martingale measure for small $\epsilon$.

steps.slogan: Combine the two directions and the uniqueness criterion.
steps.detail: The easy step shows that a martingale measure excludes arbitrage. The separation steps show that excluded arbitrage gives a martingale measure. Together they prove the first equivalence, and the uniqueness criterion proves the second for a market without arbitrage.

concepts.c:arbitrage: Absence of arbitrage is the condition that the gain subspace avoids the positive cone.
concepts.c:equivalent-measure: The measure $Q$ must charge exactly the states that $P$ charges.
concepts.c:martingale: Martingale prices under $Q$ are what the separating vector produces.

source.note: The finite-state argument of J. M. Harrison and S. R. Pliska, Stochastic Processes and their Applications 11 (1981), 215-260, with the separation step of D. M. Kreps (1981).

new_concepts.name: Arbitrage
new_concepts.reminder: An arbitrage is a trading strategy that needs no capital, never loses and wins in some state.
new_concepts.definition: An arbitrage is a self-financing strategy with initial value $0$ whose terminal gain $G$ satisfies $G\ge0$ in every state and $G>0$ with positive probability.

statement: Every square [matrix](c:matrix) $M$ over a field $k$ can be reduced to a [diagonal matrix](c:diagonal-matrix) by [elementary row](c:elementary-row-operation) and column operations that add a multiple of one line to another: there are products $L,L'$ of [transvections](c:transvection) with $LML'$ diagonal.

hypotheses.text: The [matrix](c:matrix) $M$ is square of size $n\times n$, with $n\ge0$.
The entries of $M$ lie in a field $k$.

conclusion: There are products $L,L'$ of transvection matrices and a diagonal matrix $D$ with $LML'=D$.

formal.difference: The declaration indexes rows and columns by an arbitrary finite type; this statement uses $\{1,\dots,n\}$, which is the same by reindexing.

proofs.name: Pivot and induction
proofs.slogan: Move a nonzero pivot to the corner, clear its row and column by transvections, and induct on the size of the remaining block.
proofs.scope: All sizes $n\ge0$; the empty matrix is already diagonal, and a matrix with zero first row and column skips the pivot step.

roles.why: The size $n$ drives the induction on the block that remains after the pivot.
A field allows division by the nonzero pivot, so the multiples exist.

steps.slogan: Move a nonzero entry to the corner by one transvection.
steps.detail: If the first row and column of $M$ are zero, skip this step. Otherwise some entry $M_{i0}$ or $M_{0j}$ is nonzero. If $M_{00}=0$, add that row to row $0$, or that column to column $0$; this is a [transvection](c:transvection) and gives $M_{00}\ne0$.

steps.slogan: Clear the first column and the first row with transvections.
steps.detail:
With $a=M_{00}
e0$, subtract $M_{i0}/a$ times row $0$ from row $i$ for each $i
e0$. Then subtract $M_{0j}/a$ times column $0$ from column $j$ for each $j
e0$. The result is $\mathrm{diag}(a,M')$ with $M'$ of size $n-1$.

steps.slogan: Reduce the smaller block by the induction hypothesis.
steps.detail: By induction on the size there are products $L_1,L_1'$ of transvections of size $n-1$ with $L_1M'L_1'$ diagonal. Embed them as transvections of size $n$ that act on the indices $1,\dots,n-1$ only.

steps.slogan: Multiply the transvections to obtain the diagonal form.
steps.detail: The embedded transvections fix row $0$ and column $0$ of $\mathrm{diag}(a,M')$. So the product of all transvections turns $M$ into $\mathrm{diag}(a,L_1M'L_1')$, which is diagonal.

concepts.c:matrix: The theorem reduces an arbitrary square matrix to a simpler one.
concepts.c:diagonal-matrix: Diagonal form is the goal of the reduction.
concepts.c:elementary-row-operation: Adding a multiple of one line to another is the elementary operation used.
concepts.c:transvection: Each step multiplies by a transvection matrix, an elementary operation of determinant one.

source.note: mathlib builds a two-block diagonal matrix with one pivot (exists_isTwoBlockDiagonal_list_transvec_mul_mul_list_transvec) and inducts on the size (exists_list_transvec_mul_mul_list_transvec_eq_diagonal_aux).

statement: Let $A$ be a [Banach algebra](c:banach-algebra) over $\mathbb{C}$ with unit $1\ne0$ in which every nonzero element is [invertible](c:invertible). Then $\lambda\mapsto\lambda1$ is an algebra isomorphism $\mathbb{C}\to A$.

hypotheses.text: The algebra $A$ is a unital [Banach algebra](c:banach-algebra) over $\mathbb{C}$ with $1\ne0$.
Every nonzero element of $A$ is [invertible](c:invertible).

conclusion: Every $a\in A$ equals $\lambda1$ for exactly one $\lambda\in\mathbb{C}$, so $\lambda\mapsto\lambda1$ is an algebra isomorphism $\mathbb{C}\to A$.

formal.difference: The declaration assumes that the nonzero elements are exactly the units, which gives $1\ne0$, and it uses a complete normed ring. It builds the inverse by choosing a point of the spectrum; the isometry property is the separate declaration algebraMap_isometry.

proofs.name: Nonempty spectrum
proofs.slogan: Show that every element has a spectral point by Liouville's theorem, and use invertibility of nonzero elements to turn it into a scalar.
proofs.scope: The whole statement; the zero algebra is excluded by $1\ne0$. A complex Banach [division algebra](c:division-algebra) is $\mathbb{C}$.

roles.why: Completeness gives the Neumann series, analyticity and decay of the resolvent, and $1\ne0$ gives injectivity.
Invertibility of nonzero elements turns a non-invertible $a-\lambda1$ into zero.

steps.slogan: Assume that the [spectrum](c:spectrum-of-an-operator) of $a$ is empty and form the resolvent.
steps.detail: Suppose that $a-\lambda1$ is invertible for every $\lambda\in\mathbb{C}$. Then $R(\lambda)=(a-\lambda1)^{-1}$ exists for all $\lambda$, and $R(\lambda)\ne0$ because $1\ne0$.

steps.slogan: Show that $\varphi\circ R$ is entire for every bounded functional $\varphi$.
steps.detail: The Neumann series $(1-x)^{-1}=\sum x^k$ for $\|x\|<1$ shows that inversion is analytic on the invertible elements. So $R$ is analytic, and $\varphi\circ R$ is an entire function.

steps.slogan: Show that $R(\lambda)$ is bounded and tends to $0$ at infinity.
steps.detail: For $|\lambda|>\|a\|$ write $R(\lambda)=-\lambda^{-1}(1-a/\lambda)^{-1}$, and bound the Neumann series. This gives $\|R(\lambda)\|\to0$ as $|\lambda|\to\infty$. On a large disc the continuous $R$ is bounded, so $R$ is bounded.

steps.slogan: Apply Liouville's theorem to get $R=0$ and a contradiction.
steps.detail: Each $\varphi\circ R$ is bounded and entire and tends to $0$, so it is $0$ by Liouville's theorem. The Hahn-Banach theorem then gives $R(0)=0$, which contradicts $R(0)\ne0$.

steps.slogan: Use invertibility of nonzero elements to write $a=\lambda1$.
steps.detail: So some $\lambda$ has $a-\lambda1$ not invertible. Every nonzero element is invertible, so $a-\lambda1=0$ and $a=\lambda1$.

steps.slogan: Check that $\lambda\mapsto\lambda1$ is a bijective algebra map.
steps.detail: The map is an algebra homomorphism. It is injective because $1\ne0$ in $A$, so $\lambda1=0$ forces $\lambda=0$, and it is surjective by the previous step.

concepts.c:banach-algebra: Completeness and the norm give the Neumann series and the analytic resolvent.
concepts.c:invertible: Invertibility of nonzero elements forces a non-invertible element to be zero.
concepts.c:spectrum-of-an-operator: The proof shows that the spectrum of every element is nonempty.
concepts.c:division-algebra: The theorem says the only complex Banach division algebra is $\mathbb{C}$.

source.note: mathlib picks a point of spectrum.nonempty (a Liouville argument) as the scalar, and hA turns the non-invertible a - λ1 into 0.

statement: Let $\xi$ lie in a [normed division ring](c:normed-division-ring), such as $\mathbb{R}$ or $\mathbb{C}$, with $\|\xi\|<1$. Then the [geometric series](c:geometric-series) $\sum_{n\ge0}\xi^n$ converges to $(1-\xi)^{-1}$.

hypotheses.text: The element $\xi$ lies in a [normed division ring](c:normed-division-ring), so $\|ab\|=\|a\|\|b\|$ and nonzero elements are invertible.
The norm of $\xi$ satisfies $\|\xi\|<1$.

conclusion: The series $\sum_{n\ge0}\xi^n$ converges and its sum is $(1-\xi)^{-1}$.

formal.difference: The declaration states the value of the infinite sum; convergence is the companion declaration hasSum_geometric_of_norm_lt_one, which this theorem includes.

proofs.name: Telescoping partial sums
proofs.slogan: Telescope the partial sums to $(1-\xi^n)(1-\xi)^{-1}$ and let $\xi^n$ tend to zero.
proofs.scope: The whole statement; for $\xi=0$ the series is $1$ and the proof still applies.

roles.why: Multiplicativity of the norm gives $\|\xi^n\|=\|\xi\|^n$, and the division ring allows inverting $1-\xi$.
The bound $\|\xi\|<1$ makes $\xi^n\to0$ and gives $\xi\ne1$.

steps.slogan: Telescope the [partial sum](c:partial-sum) to get $(1-\xi)S_n=1-\xi^n$.
steps.detail: Write $S_n=\sum_{k<n}\xi^k$. Multiplying out gives $(1-\xi)S_n=\sum_{k<n}(\xi^k-\xi^{k+1})=1-\xi^n$, because the inner terms cancel in pairs.

steps.slogan: Divide by $1-\xi$, which is invertible.
steps.detail: Since $\|\xi\|<1$, we have $\xi\ne1$, so $1-\xi\ne0$ and it is invertible in the division ring. Powers of $\xi$ commute with $1-\xi$, so $S_n=(1-\xi)^{-1}(1-\xi^n)$.

steps.slogan: Show that the powers $\xi^n$ tend to $0$.
steps.detail: Multiplicativity of the norm gives $\|\xi^n\|=\|\xi\|^n$. This tends to $0$ because $0\le\|\xi\|<1$.

steps.slogan: Pass to the [limit](c:limit-of-a-sequence) in the formula for $S_n$.
steps.detail: Multiplication is continuous, so $S_n=(1-\xi)^{-1}(1-\xi^n)\to(1-\xi)^{-1}$. The partial sums converge to $(1-\xi)^{-1}$, so the series converges with this sum.

concepts.c:normed-division-ring: Multiplicative norm and inverses are exactly what the proof uses.
concepts.c:geometric-series: The theorem gives the sum of this series.
concepts.c:partial-sum: The proof finds a closed form for each partial sum.
concepts.c:limit-of-a-sequence: The sum is the limit of the partial sums.

source.note: mathlib uses geom_sum_eq for the partial sums and tendsto_pow_atTop_nhds_zero_of_norm_lt_one in hasSum_geometric_of_norm_lt_one.
